prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, enabling the simultaneous interrogation of many atoms at fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep B009 with Katori and Ye as the whole configuration. After the first round my position is firmer on the science and unchanged in structure. The new element is a specific principle: a magic-wavelength optical lattice cancels the light shift, so many atoms are held in a Doppler- and recoil-free regime and the statistical power of an ensemble is combined with the systematic control of a single trapped particle. That is a different mechanism from the frequency comb (2005), which only counts optical cycles, and from single-ion control (2012). The experimental evidence is what I look for in a prize. Sr, Yb and Hg lattice clocks built independently at RIKEN, JILA, PTB, NIST and SYRTE agree in international comparisons at about 1e-18, and they are already used for millimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurements and bounds on drifting constants. I would put the citation on the lattice principle and the precision it reached, and leave the redefinition of the second out of it. That redefinition is a consequence that may still be delayed. The statement of precision matters as the demonstrated result, not as the claim that every clock is now better.
statement.case_against: The overlap with 2005 and 2012 is real and I do not think the committee should wave it away. The lattice clock reads the comb for its frequency output, and a hostile reader can call the prize a third metrology award in one lineage, for a record number and not for a deviation from known physics. My answer is that the citation must name the lattice principle and not clock accuracy in general. If an outside reviewer told us the magic-wavelength idea was not Katori's, or that Ye's decisive contribution is the wider JILA programme and not the lattice clock itself, I would reopen the credit. The names outside the pair (Lemonde, Ludlow, Oates, Takamoto) also remain a risk that two names cannot fully remove. Finally, I am an astroparticle experimentalist and I am judging atomic physics through colleagues and reviewers.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked B009 only sixth in the opening because it is not the discovery of a new state of matter, and is less relaxed about the 2012 ion-clock overlap than about the 2005 comb.
responses.response: I agree that 2012 is the closer precedent and I do not want to dismiss it. I do not accept that a prize needs a new state of matter. A clean instrument that opens a measurement regime and then yields physics, here many-body spin exchange in the lattice and relativistic redshift over millimetres, is within the Nobel tradition I know from detector work. The difference from 2012 is a different principle, the many-atom magic-wavelength lattice rather than control of one ion, and this should be said in the citation. What would settle it for me is Eriksson's own reading of the many-body results. If you still hold it back, tell us whether your objection is to the overlap or to the lack of a new state of matter, because I answer them differently.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B005 to B009 because of the single mechanism (a magic wavelength cancels the lattice light shift), the independent replication and the consistency checks that clock comparisons provide.
responses.response: We agree, and I want to keep the wording you chose, magic-wavelength trapping, in the citation. I would be careful with your point that all eight of us proposed exactly Katori and Ye. That is a statement about our agreement and not evidence about priority. Several of us said we rely on memory, so I would not cite it in the record as a verification of credit. The check should come from a reviewer who can trace Katori's proposal and first demonstration, and the later JILA milestones, to a source.

responses.point: Johansson notes that no deviation from known physics has been found, so the prize would reward a record-setting instrument, and that the answer lies in the citation naming the magic-wavelength lattice.
responses.response: I agree on the wording. I would add that the lack of a deviation from theory does not weaken a measurement of this kind. A comparison between clocks at the 1e-18 level that agrees across species and laboratories is a quantitative confirmation of general relativity at millimetre scales and of constant fundamental constants, and the null result is part of the physics. I would therefore keep the precision figure in the citation as the demonstrated result and keep out the redefinition of the second and any dark-matter search, which are prospective. Your note about Lemonde, PTB and Oates is the point I would most like an outside expert to answer in writing before the vote.

responses.point: Lindroth states that within the atomic community the magic-wavelength priority is not seriously contested as Katori's, and that Katori's and Ye's roles are separable.
responses.response: That helps, and I take it as the view of the one member with real atomic-physics standing, not as a checked fact. I accept the Katori half. The Ye half is where I still need an answer. If his decisive contribution is the strontium lattice clock reaching the 1e-18 level with a systematic-uncertainty evaluation, then the credit is clean. If it is the broader JILA programme with the comb-linked spectroscopy, then Hall's 2005 prize bears on how we frame his share and we should say so. Your answer on this will weigh more than mine.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether the redefinition of the second and the new-physics searches count as realised or still prospective impact, and flags a year of his PhD in John Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: My view is that they are prospective, and the committee should rest the case only on what is realised: independent reproduction, the millimetre-scale redshift measurement and the bounds on drifting constants. On your disclosure, I do not consider a year in Hall's laboratory as a reason for you to step back, since it is a loose connection to Ye's environment and you have said so openly. I would only ask that you not be the member who reports on the Ye credit, so that the answer comes from someone without that link.

uncertainties: Whether Jun Ye's credit is for the lattice clock specifically or for the wider JILA programme, and whether Hall's 2005 prize affects the framing of his share.
Whether the committee, and especially Eriksson, accepts that the many-atom magic-wavelength lattice is distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether Lemonde, Ludlow, Oates, Takamoto and other early lattice-clock contributors can be left out of a two-name credit without an outside priority review.

Atomic physics is outside my expertise, so I depend on the reviewers. If B009 were set aside, my reserves are B010, which needs a choice of three of four names, and B052, where the credit cannot represent the collaboration or the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND pioneers.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict for B009. As Chair I have no connection to Katori or Ye. My general field closeness to B052 (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur membership) is unchanged, I name no personal tie to its credited people, and since B052 is only a reserve I do not see a need to recuse. I have no disclosure to add after round 1: Kroll's loose Hall link and Johansson's possible B008 conflict were noted by them, and I do not think either changes the B009 case.
